questions.title: Can a fair‑use defense be raised as a decisive affirmative defense at the pleading stage under Rule 12(b)(6)?
questions.question_body: In Santos v. Kimmel the Second Circuit affirmed dismissal of the copyright claims on a Rule 12(b)(6) basis because fair use was ‘so clearly established by the complaint.’ I thought affirmative defenses like fair use are typically considered later, after discovery. How can a court decide that fair use bars a claim before any evidence beyond the pleadings is presented? What standards do courts apply to determine that a fair‑use defense is evident on the face of the complaint?

questions.title: How does the ‘reasonable observer’ test determine whether a secondary use is transformative when the defendant actually prompted creation of the original work?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that Kimmel ‘instigated the creation’ of Santos’s videos and therefore ‘is the designer’ of their original purpose, yet still finds the use transformative based on what a reasonable observer would think. How do courts balance a defendant’s role in prompting creation against the objective ‘reasonable observer’ standard? Are there precedents that clarify how much weight is given to who originated the original work in assessing transformation?

questions.title: What is the current relevance of Harper & Row’s ‘good faith’ requirement in fair‑use analysis, and why did this court reject it?
questions.question_body: Santos argues that Kimmel’s false representations show bad faith, invoking Harper & Row’s statement that ‘fair use presupposes good faith.’ The Second Circuit says later cases have distanced from that language and declines to apply it here. Which decisions have limited Harper & Row’s good‑faith prong, and under what circumstances (if any) does good faith still factor into a fair‑use determination?

questions.title: When are state‐law breach‑of‑contract claims preempted by the Copyright Act?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed Santos’s breach‑of‑contract and implied‑contract claims as preempted, yet did not reach merits because they allegedly failed to state a claim. How do courts analyze statutory preemption for contractual claims related to copyrighted works? Does simply alleging breach of an online platform’s terms automatically trigger preemption, or must there be more specific overlap with exclusive rights?

questions.title: Can a non‑signatory enforce provisions of an online Terms of Service as a third‑party beneficiary under Illinois law?
questions.question_body: Santos was not a party to Cameo’s Terms of Service but sued based on alleged breaches of those terms. The opinion cites Illinois’s strong presumption against granting benefits to non‑contracting third parties unless there is an express declaration. What criteria must be satisfied for a non‑signatory like Santos to be considered an intended third‑party beneficiary, and how do courts interpret ‘express declaration’ in website terms?

questions.title: How do courts resolve conflicts when different states govern different aspects of a contract claim (e.g., Illinois for TOS vs. New York for implied contract)?
questions.question_body: In this case, Illinois law was applied to evaluate whether Santos could rely on Cameo’s Terms of Service, while New York law governed the alleged breach of implied contract claim. What choice‑of‑law principles guide courts in such mixed jurisdictional scenarios, and can one state’s doctrine on third‑party beneficiaries override another state’s substantive contract analysis?

questions.title: What constitutes ‘out‑of‑pocket loss’ for a fraudulent inducement claim in New York, and can intangible harms like reputational damage satisfy this element?
questions.question_body: The appellate court affirmed dismissal of Santos’s fraudulent inducement claim because he did not allege any out‑of‑pocket loss. Under New York law, what types of losses qualify as out‑of‑pocket? If a plaintiff suffers damage to reputation or lost future revenue opportunities due to fraud, can those be pleaded as sufficient losses, or must they be strictly monetary expenditures incurred at the time of fraud?
